title: Using Structs
objectives: Define and return named, tuple and unit-like structs; read and mutate fields.
Use field shorthand and struct update while predicting partial moves.
Distinguish a non-Copy numeric struct from an explicitly Copy one.
Clone owned text independently and understand field requirements for derives.
Write read, mutate and consuming methods with explicit ownership behavior.
Use constructors, Self and multiple impl blocks.

lessons.title: Defining and creating structs
lessons.book_section: 5.1 Defining and Instantiating Structs (up to and including Using the Field Init Shorthand)
lessons.objective_md: After this lesson the learner can define a struct with named fields, create an instance with every field, read and change fields, use field init shorthand, and explain why struct fields usually own their data.

screens.heading: Related values belong together
screens.text_md:
A **struct** groups several related values under one name. Each value is a **field**, and every field has a name and a type.

With a tuple you'd have to remember that position 2 is the email. With a struct you just ask for `email`.

Struct names use `PascalCase`, like `User`. Field names use `snake_case`, like `sign_in_count`.

coming_from.c: Very close to a C `struct`. Two differences: you must initialise every field (there are no garbage values), and you always use `.` to reach a field, never `->`.
coming_from.go: Almost the same as a Go struct. The difference: Rust struct literals require explicit field initialization. Default is an explicit capability taught in L5.3.
coming_from.java: A struct is like a Java `record` or a C# class with only fields. There's no `new` keyword and no constructor by default: you write `User { ... }` and give every field a value.
coming_from.js: A struct is like a TypeScript `interface` plus a matching object literal, but it's a concrete compiled type. You must give every field when you create one, and you can't add new properties later.
coming_from.python: A struct is like a Python `@dataclass`: named fields, each with a type. Unlike Python, the set of fields is fixed when you compile. You can't add `user1.age = 30` later.

steps.caption_md: The `struct` definition is only a blueprint. It says which fields a `User` has, but no `User` exists yet.
steps.visual_md: Type `User`: active: bool, username: String, email: String, sign_in_count: u64; Instances: none; stdout: empty

steps.caption_md: `User { ... }` creates an **instance**. You give every field a value as `name: value`. The order doesn't have to match the definition.
steps.visual_md: Owner `user1`: active=true, username="ferris", email="ferris@example.com", sign_in_count=1; stdout: empty

steps.caption_md: Dot notation reads one field: `user1.email`. This line prints `ferris@example.com`.
steps.visual_md: Read `user1.email`: "ferris@example.com"; Owner `user1`: still available; stdout: ferris@example.com

screens.heading: Changing a field needs `mut`
screens.text_md:
For ordinary field assignment, `mut` applies to the binding or access path, not to individual field declarations.

To change any field, declare the variable with `let mut`. Then `user1.email = ...` works.
screens.diagnostic:
error[E0594]: cannot assign to `user1.email`, as `user1` is not declared as mutable
  --> src/main.rs:15:5
   |
15 |     user1.email = String::from("crab@example.com");
   |     ^^^^^^^^^^^ cannot assign
   |
help: consider changing this to be mutable
   |
 9 |     let mut user1 = User {
   |         +++

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0594`.

explanations.text_md: Correct. `c` is declared with `let mut`, so any of its fields can be changed. It prints `clicks = 1`.
Not quite. This code mutates an owned local c. Its `let mut` binding supplies the required mutable access; no move or conflicting borrow occurs.

screens.heading: Building a struct in a function
screens.text_md:
Creating an instance is an expression, so a function can return one. The last expression in `build_user` is the new `User`, with no semicolon.

The two `String`s passed in move into the new struct's fields. The function hands the finished `User` back, and `main` owns it. This prints `ferris <ferris@example.com>`.

screens.heading: Field init shorthand
screens.text_md: `username,` means exactly `username: username,`. This is called **field init shorthand**. You can mix both styles in one instance, as `active: true` shows.

left.label: Name repeated
left.caption_md: `username: username` says the same name twice.

right.label: Field init shorthand
right.caption_md: When a variable has the same name as the field, write it once.

steps.caption_md: `name` owns the text `ferris` on the heap.
steps.visual_md: Owner `name` → buffer "ferris"; String metadata: length=6 bytes, capacity≥6; user1: not yet constructed

steps.caption_md: `username: name` moves the `String` into the struct. Now `user1` owns both texts through its fields, and `name` can't be used.
steps.visual_md: `name`: moved; `user1.username` → existing buffer "ferris" (6 bytes); `user1.email` → buffer "ferris@example.com" (18 bytes); user1.active=true, user1.sign_in_count=1

steps.caption_md: When `user1` goes out of scope, Rust drops it, and every field with it. Both heap texts are freed, exactly once.
steps.visual_md: Scope ended: `user1` drops its owned fields; Buffers "ferris" and "ferris@example.com": released; Moved `name`: owns no buffer to release

question.prompt_md: Fill in the blank using field init shorthand, so `make_book` puts its `title` parameter into the `title` field.
question.general_md: Correct. `title` abbreviates `title: title`, moving the owned parameter into the new Book. The `pages` field already uses the same shorthand.

wrong_answers.answer_md: Not quite. `String` is a type name, not the parameter value that belongs in this field.
Not quite. `title.clone()` is not shorthand; this task transfers the supplied owned value without an extra clone.

screens.heading: Why `String` and not `&str`?
screens.text_md:
While a struct owns a `String` field, it keeps that field’s data alive. Moving the field out transfers responsibility separately; printing the field only reads it.

A reference field borrows data someone else owns, so Rust must check that the data lives long enough. That needs lifetimes. Until Chapter 10, give your struct fields owned types.

error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier

  |
3 |     username: &str,
  |               ^ expected named lifetime parameter
  |
help: consider introducing a named lifetime parameter
  |
1 ~ struct User<'a> {
2 |     active: bool,
3 ~     username: &'a str,
  |

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0106`.

screens.heading: Numeric fields do not automatically mean Copy
screens.text_md: This numeric-only struct needs no owned heap buffer, yet Count does not implement Copy. The right-hand value moves from s2 into s1. Reading s2 afterward would be E0382. Copy capability is a type rule, not a physical placement rule.

steps.caption_md: Before initialization, s2 owns the numeric struct.
steps.visual_md: Bindings: s2 owns Count { n:3 }; s1 absent; Data: No heap allocation is required by these fields.

steps.caption_md: let s1=s2 initializes s1 by moving the whole Count. The later print copies its u32 field. Being fixed-size does not make Count Copy.
steps.visual_md: Bindings: s1 owns Count { n:3 }; s2 moved; Data: Same numeric value; no duplicated owner is introduced.

screens.heading: Replacing an owned struct
screens.text_md: Assignment flows from the right-hand source to the left-hand destination. Replacement needs a mutable destination; the source need not be mutable. Replacing s1 drops its old String, then transfers s2 and its field ownership. Initialization and replacement are different operations.

steps.caption_md: Before replacement, both owned values are initialized.
steps.visual_md: Bindings: s1 owns old; s2 owns incoming; Data: Two independently owned String buffers.

steps.caption_md: After s1=s2, the old destination is cleaned up. Printing borrows the String field; it does not move it.
steps.visual_md: Bindings: s1 owns incoming; s2 moved; Data: old buffer released; incoming buffer remains owned.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. A numeric-only custom struct still moves without Copy.
Correct. A numeric-only custom struct still moves without Copy.

summary: Define a named type, initialize every field, and read or mutate through the correct binding.
Use field shorthand and return owned structs without dangling data.
A numeric-only custom struct can move; replacing an owner drops its previous owned fields.

lessons.title: Tuple structs, unit structs and struct update
lessons.book_section: 5.1 Creating Instances with Struct Update Syntax; Creating Different Types with Tuple Structs; Defining Unit-Like Structs
lessons.objective_md: After this lesson the learner can build an instance from another with `..`, predict which fields move, define and use tuple structs and newtypes, and recognise unit-like structs.

screens.heading: Reusing fields from another instance
screens.text_md:
`..user1` means "take every field I didn't list from `user1`". This is **struct update syntax**.

The `..user1` part must come last, after the fields you set yourself, and it has no comma after it.

left.label: Every field by hand
left.caption_md: Works, but you repeat every field you don't change.

right.label: Struct update syntax
right.caption_md: List only what changes; `..user1` fills in the rest.

coming_from.c: A generated C++ memberwise copy copies its std::string members as independent strings. Rust struct update copies Copy fields and moves other reused fields; clone explicitly when independent owned text is needed.
coming_from.go: In Go, `u2 := u1; u2.Email = "..."` copies the struct and both share the string data. Rust moves the `String` fields, so the old instance can't use them any more.
coming_from.java: It's like C#'s `user1 with { Email = "..." }` for records. C# shares the same string objects; Rust moves `String` fields, so the old instance loses them.
coming_from.js: It looks like `{ ...user1, email: "..." }`, but the spread comes last, uses two dots, and moves `String` fields instead of sharing references.
coming_from.python: It's like `dataclasses.replace(user1, email="...")`, except Rust moves the `String` fields out of `user1` instead of sharing them, so `user1.username` becomes unusable.

steps.caption_md: `user1` owns two heap texts through its `username` and `email` fields.
steps.visual_md: `user1.username` → "ferris"; `user1.email` → "ferris@example.com"; user1.active=true, user1.sign_in_count=1

steps.caption_md: `..user1` fills `active`, `username` and `sign_in_count`. The `bool` and the `u64` are copied. The `username` `String` is **moved**: `user2` owns `ferris` now.
steps.visual_md: `user1.username`: moved into user2; `user1.email` → "ferris@example.com" remains; `user2.username` → existing "ferris" buffer; `user2.email` → new "crab@example.com" buffer; Both active=true and sign_in_count=1

steps.caption_md: `user1.email` and `user1.sign_in_count` still work: `email` was never moved, and `u64` is `Copy`. Only `user1.username`, and `user1` as a whole, can't be used.
steps.visual_md: Usable reads: user1.email, user1.sign_in_count, user2.username; Unavailable: user1.username and the whole user1 value; stdout lines: ferris@example.com / 1 / ferris

question.prompt_md: `User` has the fields `active: bool`, `username: String`, `email: String` and `sign_in_count: u64`. After this code, which of these can still be used? (Select all that apply.)

options.text_md: `user1` as a whole, e.g. passed to a function

explanations.text_md: Correct. `email` was given a new value, so `..user1` never touched `user1.email`.
Correct. `active` is a `bool`, which is `Copy`, so it was copied, not moved.
Not quite. `username` is a `String` that `..user1` moved into `user2`.
Not quite. Part of `user1` has moved out, so `user1` can no longer be used as a whole.

screens.heading: Tuple structs: a name, but no field names
screens.text_md:
A **tuple struct** has a name, but its fields don't. You read them by position, `.0`, `.1`, `.2`, just like a tuple. You can also take one apart: `let Point(x, y, z) = origin;`.

Use one when naming every field adds nothing, but the whole value deserves its own type. This program prints `0 0`, then `0 0 0`.

screens.heading: Same fields, different types
screens.text_md:
`Color` and `Point` hold the same data, but Rust treats them as different types.

Wrapping a single value in its own tuple struct, like `struct Meters(f64);`, is called a **newtype**. The compiler then catches mix-ups, such as passing meters where seconds are expected.
screens.diagnostic:
error[E0308]: mismatched types
  --> src/main.rs:10:16
   |
10 |     show_point(black);
   |     ---------- ^^^^^ expected `Point`, found `Color`
   |     |
   |     arguments to this function are incorrect
   |
note: function defined here
  --> src/main.rs:4:4
   |
 4 | fn show_point(p: Point) {
   |    ^^^^^^^^^^ --------

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0308`.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. Both wrap one `f64`, but `Celsius` and `Fahrenheit` are different types. Rust does not implicitly convert one named tuple struct into the other.
Correct. Line 6 tries to store a `Celsius` in a variable of type `Fahrenheit`. That mix-up is exactly what newtypes are for catching.

screens.heading: Unit-like structs
screens.text_md:
A **unit-like struct** has no fields at all. You define it with a name and a semicolon, and you create a value by writing its name: `AlwaysEqual`.

It holds no data, but it's still a type of its own. That becomes useful in Chapter 10, when you give types behaviour with traits. The name comes from the unit type `()`.

screens.heading: Three shapes of struct
screens.text_md:
Use **named fields** when each value needs a name. Use a **tuple struct** when position is enough, or to give one value its own type. Use a **unit-like struct** when you need a type but no data.

This program prints `Ana 31 4.5`.

question.prompt_md: In a struct literal that explicitly sets `email` and takes the other fields from `base`, where does `..base` belong?

options.text_md: Before `email`, so the explicit field can override it later.
Last, after the explicitly supplied fields.
In every field that should be copied.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. Unlike some object-spread syntaxes, Rust's struct-update base must appear last in the literal.
Correct. Write the explicit email field first and `..base` last; update supplies the omitted fields according to their move or Copy behavior.
Not quite. One update expression supplies omitted fields. It is not written separately beside each field.

summary: Tuple structs give distinct types to positional fields; unit-like structs have no fields.
Struct update fills only omitted fields and can partially move an instance.
Untouched owned fields and copied numeric fields remain usable after a partial move.

lessons.title: A program with structs, and derived traits
lessons.book_section: 5.2 An Example Program Using Structs (plus Appendix C: Derivable Traits)
lessons.objective_md: After this lesson the learner can refactor loose values into a struct, print a struct with `{:?}`, `{:#?}` and `dbg!`, and choose which of `Debug`, `Clone`, `Copy`, `PartialEq`, `Eq` and `Default` to derive.

screens.heading: Refactor loose values and tuples into a named struct
screens.text_md:
Both programs print `Area: 1500`, and both work. But neither says clearly what the numbers mean.

The goal: one value that is a rectangle, with a width and a height you can ask for by name.

left.label: Two loose numbers
left.caption_md: Nothing says that `width1` and `height1` belong together.

right.label: A tuple
right.caption_md: Grouped now, but which one is the width? `.0` and `.1` don't say.

screens.heading: Debug and Display are separate capabilities
screens.text_md:
Numbers and strings know how to display themselves. Your own struct doesn't, because there are many ways to show a rectangle.

The compiler suggests `{:?}`. Let's try it.

coming_from.c: C and C++ have no built-in way to print a struct; you'd write an `operator<<` or a print function. `#[derive(Debug)]` generates that code for you.
coming_from.go: `{:?}` is like Go's `%+v`, and `{:#?}` like a pretty-printed dump. Go can print any struct; Rust needs `#[derive(Debug)]` first.
coming_from.java: Like overriding `toString()`, except the compiler writes it when you add `#[derive(Debug)]`. There's no default like Java's `User@1b6d3586`; without it, the code doesn't compile.
coming_from.js: `console.log(obj)` prints any object. Rust won't print a struct until you derive `Debug`; then `{:?}` shows a similar field-by-field view.
coming_from.python: `{:?}` is like `repr()` and `{}` like `str()`. Python gives every object a default `repr`; Rust gives a struct none until you derive `Debug`.

error[E0277]: `Rectangle` doesn't implement `std::fmt::Display`

   |                        ^^^^^^^^^ `Rectangle` cannot be formatted using `{:?}` because it doesn't implement `Debug`

   = note: add `#[derive(Debug)]` to `Rectangle` or manually `impl Debug for Rectangle`
help: consider annotating `Rectangle` with `#[derive(Debug)]`

 1 + #[derive(Debug)]

   |

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0277`.

steps.caption_md: `#[derive(Debug)]` gives `Rectangle` the Debug format.
steps.visual_md: Type Rectangle: width:u32, height:u32; Capability: derived Debug; stdout: empty

steps.caption_md: `{:?}` prints the struct on one line: its name, then each field with its value.
steps.visual_md: rect1: width=30, height=50; Compact stdout: rect1 is Rectangle { width: 30, height: 50 }

steps.caption_md: `{:#?}` is **pretty** Debug: one field per line. It's easier to read for bigger structs.
steps.visual_md: rect1 remains width=30, height=50; Additional pretty stdout: rect1 is Rectangle { ↵ width: 30, ↵ height: 50, ↵ }

question.general_md: Correct. Derived Debug prints the type name and named fields: `Point { x: 3, y: -1 }`. The debug marker `:?` asks for this representation.

wrong_answers.answer_md: Not quite. `3 -1` would require printing the two fields separately; this print formats the whole Point.
Not quite. A Display error would occur with `{p}`. The written `{p:?}` uses the derived Debug capability.

screens.heading: `dbg!`: print where a value came from

steps.caption_md: `dbg!` prints the file, the line, the expression and its value. Then it **returns** the value, so `width` still gets 60.
steps.visual_md: scale=2, rect1.width=60; stderr: [src/main.rs:10:16] 30 * scale = 60; Returned dbg! value: 60

steps.caption_md: `dbg!` receives its argument by value and returns that value; a non-`Copy` argument moves in and back out. It, so pass `&rect1` when you want to inspect without moving `rect1`. It writes to **standard error**, which keeps debug notes apart from your program's normal output.
steps.visual_md: rect1: Rectangle { width: 60, height: 50 }; stderr also contains the borrowed Rectangle diagnostic at src/main.rs:13:5; Ownership: rect1 remains with its caller

screens.heading: `==` needs `PartialEq`
screens.text_md:
Deriving `Debug` doesn't give you `==`. Each ability comes from its own trait.

With `PartialEq` derived, two rectangles are equal when every field is equal, so this would print `true`.

screens.heading: Compare numeric structs with and without Copy
screens.text_md: Copy is an explicit capability of the custom type. All fields must support Copy, and Copy also requires Clone. a remains usable after assignment, with independent numeric fields. x moved into y despite having the same kind of numeric field.

steps.caption_md: The CopyCount assignment copies; both numeric instances are independently usable.
steps.visual_md: Bindings: a:3; b:3; x not initialized yet; Data: Numeric values only; heap allocation is not the deciding factor.

steps.caption_md: Changing b does not change a. Using x would be rejected.
steps.visual_md: Bindings: a:3; b:9; x moved; y:4; Data: Independent copied scalar values; one transferred MoveCount.

question.prompt_md: A struct is declared with `#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]` and nothing else. For two values `a` and `b` of this struct, which lines compile? (Select all that apply.)

explanations.text_md: Correct. `Debug` gives the `{:?}` format.
Correct. `PartialEq` gives `==`.
Not quite. `.clone()` needs `Clone`, which isn't in the derive list.
Correct. `PartialEq` gives `!=` as well as `==`.
Not quite. `{}` needs `Display`; neither of the shown standard derives supplies that capability.

screens.heading: Clone owned fields independently
screens.text_md: Derived Clone calls each field’s clone implementation. For String this creates independently owned text. This is not a universal promise that every Clone implementation recursively duplicates everything: later pointer types can clone shared handles.

steps.caption_md: Explicit clone preserves the original and creates another owned String.
steps.visual_md: Bindings: a owns hi; b owns hi; Data: Two independent owned text buffers.

steps.caption_md: Changing either field leaves the other unchanged.
steps.visual_md: Bindings: a owns hiA; b owns hiB; Data: Both buffers can grow independently; exact capacity and addresses are unspecified.

screens.heading: A String field cannot be Copy
screens.text_md: This is an intentionally rejected program. String does not implement Copy; therefore a struct that owns String cannot derive Copy. It may derive Clone and move normally. Compare the actual E0204 diagnostic with the valid Clone-only example.
screens.diagnostic:
error[E0204]: the trait `Copy` cannot be implemented for this type
 --> src/main.rs:2:8
  |
1 | #[derive(Clone,Copy)]
  |                ---- in this derive macro expansion
2 | struct Label { text:String }
  |        ^^^^^   ----------- this field does not implement `Copy`

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0204`.

screens.heading: PartialEq, Eq and floating-point limits
screens.text_md:
`PartialEq` enables field-by-field `==` and `!=`. `Eq` adds the promise that every value equals itself; it requires `PartialEq` and every field type must support `Eq`.

The numeric Ticket can derive both. A floating-point field supports `PartialEq` but not `Eq`: NaN is unequal to itself. Even if a particular Reading currently contains 0.0, its field type remains f64, so deriving Eq for the type is still rejected. Copy, Clone, Debug and equality are separate capabilities.

screens.heading: Default chooses each field’s default
screens.text_md:
`#[derive(Default)]` builds an instance by asking each field type for its default. It works only when every field type supports Default. For the types here, the String is empty, the bool is false and the u32 is zero. This is a per-field operation, not a promise to fill arbitrary memory with zero bytes.

`Preferences::default()` is a call on the type. It creates a value without an existing receiver; L5.5 develops this associated-call syntax. Deriving Default does not automatically create a function named new.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. String is not Copy, so the derive is rejected.
Correct. String is not Copy, so the derive is rejected.

verify.error_message: error[E0204]: the trait `Copy` cannot be implemented for this type

summary: Debug formats programmer output; dbg! writes to stderr and returns its argument.
Copy must be explicit and requires Copy fields plus Clone; String fields cannot be Copy.
Derived Clone clones each field; String clones own independent text.
PartialEq compares fields, Eq excludes NaN-based floating equality, and Default uses field defaults.

lessons.title: Methods
lessons.book_section: 5.3 Method Syntax; Methods with More Parameters
lessons.objective_md: After this lesson the learner can define methods in an `impl` block, choose between `&self`, `&mut self` and `self`, call methods with dot syntax, and write methods that take extra parameters.

screens.heading: From function to method
screens.text_md:
A **method** is a function defined inside an `impl` block for a type. Its first parameter is always `self`: the instance it was called on.

Both programs print `1500`. The method version keeps the behaviour next to the type, and you call it with `rect1.area()`.

coming_from.c: Like C++ member functions: `&self` is like a `const` method, `&mut self` like a non-const one. The `.` operator borrows for you, so there's no `->`.
coming_from.go: Very close to Go methods: `&self` and `&mut self` are like pointer receivers `(r *Rect)`, and `self` like a value receiver, except Rust moves the value instead of copying it.
coming_from.java: Like instance methods, with `this` written out as `self` in the parameter list. There are no classes: fields live in the `struct`, methods in an `impl` block.
coming_from.js: Like class methods, but `self` is written explicitly instead of JavaScript's hidden `this`. The data (`struct`) and the behaviour (`impl`) are declared in separate blocks.
coming_from.python: Like a Python method, `self` is written out in the definition. Rust adds a choice Python doesn't have: `&self`, `&mut self` or `self` decides whether the method reads, changes or consumes the instance.

left.label: A function
left.caption_md: You have to know `area` exists, and pass the rectangle in.

right.label: A method
right.caption_md: `area` belongs to `Rectangle` and is called with a dot.

steps.caption_md: `impl Rectangle { ... }` is an **implementation block**. Every function inside it belongs to `Rectangle`.
steps.visual_md: Type Rectangle: width:u32, height:u32; Method: area(&self) -> u32

steps.caption_md: `&self` is short for `self: &Self`. Inside an `impl` block, `Self` means the type being implemented, here `Rectangle`. So `area` borrows the rectangle.
steps.visual_md: Receiver shorthand: &self = self: &Self; In this impl: Self = Rectangle

steps.caption_md: `rect1.area()` passes `rect1` as `self`. Rust adds the `&` for you: this is **automatic referencing**. It means the same as `Rectangle::area(&rect1)`.

lessons.title: Associated functions and multiple `impl` blocks
lessons.objective_md: After this lesson the learner can write and call associated functions such as constructors, use `Self`, tell when to use `::` versus `.`, and split methods across several `impl` blocks.

screens.heading: Functions without `self`
screens.text_md:
Every function in an `impl` block is an **associated function**: it belongs to the type. One without `self` isn't a method, because there's no instance to call it on.

You call it on the type, with `::`: `Rectangle::square(3)`. This program prints `Rectangle { width: 3, height: 3 }`.

screens.heading: Constructors are usually called `new`
screens.text_md:
Rust has no special constructor syntax. By convention, an associated function called `new` builds an instance. It can fill in fields the caller shouldn't have to think about, like `count: 0`.

You've already used associated functions: `String::new()` and `String::from("hi")`. This program prints `10`.

coming_from.c: Like `static` member functions, called with `::` as in C++. Rust has no constructors: `new` is a normal function returning `Self`, so there are no half-built objects.
coming_from.go: Like Go's `NewCounter(5)` convention, but the function lives in the type's `impl` block and is called as `Counter::new(5)`.
coming_from.java: Associated functions are Rust's `static` methods, and `new` is a static factory method by convention, not a keyword. You call them with `::` instead of `.`.
coming_from.js: Like a `static` method on a class. There's no `new` keyword and no `constructor`: `Counter::new(5)` is just a function that returns a `Counter`.
coming_from.python: `Counter::new(5)` plays the role of `Counter(5)` calling `__init__`, but `new` is an ordinary function you write. Associated functions without `self` are like `@staticmethod`s.

screens.heading: Several `impl` blocks
screens.text_md:
A type can have any number of `impl` blocks. All their functions belong to the same type, exactly as if you'd written one block. Two functions with the same name would still clash.

There's no reason to split here. Separate blocks become useful in Chapter 10, with generic types and traits. This prints `20 true`.

screens.heading: `::` or `.`?
screens.text_md:
Ask whether the function takes a receiver. A method takes `self` and is normally called as `value.method(...)`. A receiver-free associated function is called as `Type::function(...)`, even when you already have other instances.

A method can also be called the long way: `Rectangle::area(&sq)` means the same as `sq.area()`.

problems.title: Grid distance
problems.description_md:
A city map is a grid of streets. A `Point` has an `x` and a `y` (both `i32`, and both can be negative). A taxi can only drive along the grid, so the distance between two points is the **Manhattan distance**: `|a.x - b.x| + |a.y - b.y|`.

Write:

- `manhattan(a, b)`: the Manhattan distance as a `u64`. Points can be anywhere in the `i32` range, so do the arithmetic in a wider type (`i64`); the result always fits in a `u64`.
- `is_adjacent(a, b)`: `true` when the two points are exactly 1 apart (one step up, down, left or right). A point is not adjacent to itself, and diagonal neighbours (distance 2) are not adjacent. There is no wrap-around at the edges of the `i32` range.
problems.examples_md:
```
Input:  manhattan(&Point { x: 1, y: 2 }, &Point { x: 4, y: 6 })
Output: 7
3 steps across plus 4 steps up.

Input:  is_adjacent(&Point { x: 0, y: 0 }, &Point { x: 0, y: 1 })
Output: true
One step up.
```
problems.constraints_md: - `i32::MIN ≤ x, y ≤ i32::MAX`.
hints: Read the fields with `a.x`, `b.y` and so on.
`a.x - b.x` can overflow `i32` (think of `i32::MAX - i32::MIN`). Convert first: `a.x as i64`.
`let dx = (a.x as i64 - b.x as i64).abs() as u64;` and the same for `dy`; then `is_adjacent` is `manhattan(a, b) == 1`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Cast each coordinate to `i64`, subtract, take `.abs()`, cast to `u64`, add the two. The largest possible sum is `2 × (2³² − 1)`, which fits a `u64`. `is_adjacent` returns `manhattan(a, b) == 1`.

problems.title: Colour codes
problems.description_md:
Web pages write colours as hex codes such as `"#ff8000"`: red `ff` (255), green `80` (128), blue `00` (0). A colour is the tuple struct `Rgb(red, green, blue)` (given). Write three functions.

`to_hex(c)` returns the code as `#` followed by six **lowercase** hex digits, two per channel, with a leading zero when needed: `Rgb(1, 2, 3)` is `"#010203"`.

`parse_hex(s)` reads a code. First remove whitespace from both ends (`trim`). The rest is valid only if it is `#` followed by **exactly 3 or exactly 6** ASCII hex digits (`0`–`9`, `a`–`f`, `A`–`F`):

- 6 digits: two per channel, `"#1E90ff"` is `Rgb(30, 144, 255)`.
- 3 digits: each digit is doubled, `"#abc"` means `"#aabbcc"`, which is `Rgb(170, 187, 204)`.

Return `(true, colour)` for a valid code. For anything else, including `""`, a missing `#`, a wrong number of digits, a sign such as `+`, or any non-ASCII character, return `(false, Rgb(0, 0, 0))`. (The `bool` is needed because `Rgb(0, 0, 0)` is also a real colour, black. Chapter 6 shows a better way with `Option`.)

`mix(a, b)` returns the average of the two colours, channel by channel, rounded down: `(a.0 + b.0) / 2` computed without overflow.

```
Input:  to_hex(Rgb(255, 128, 0))

Input:  parse_hex("#1E90ff")

Upper- and lowercase digits are both fine.

Input:  mix(Rgb(255, 0, 0), Rgb(0, 0, 255))

255 / 2 rounds down to 127.
```

- `largest(rects)`: the rectangle with the largest area. If several share the largest area, return the **first** of them. If the slice is empty, return `Rect { width: 0, height: 0 }`.
- `count_fitting(rects, space)`: how many rectangles fit inside `space`. A rectangle fits if `width ≤ space.width` and `height ≤ space.height`, **or** it fits after turning it 90° (`height ≤ space.width` and `width ≤ space.height`). Equal sizes fit.

```
Input:  count_fitting(&[Rect { width: 2, height: 3 }, Rect { width: 3, height: 2 }, Rect { width: 4, height: 1 }], &Rect { width: 3, height: 3 })
Output: 2
4 is wider than 3 both ways round.

Input:  area(&Rect { width: 4, height: 5 })
```

problems.description_md:
In a game, each inventory slot holds up to `max` items of one kind. Write these methods on `Slot`:

- `add(&mut self, n) -> u32`: adds as many of the `n` items as fit (the count never goes above `max`) and returns how many did **not** fit.
- `take(&mut self, n) -> u32`: removes up to `n` items and returns how many were actually removed. The `item` name stays even when the count reaches 0.
- `is_full(&self) -> bool`: `true` when `count == max` (so an empty slot with `max` 0 is full).
- `same_item(&self, other) -> bool`: `true` when the two slots hold the same item, comparing names after Unicode lowercasing (`to_lowercase`), so `"Épée"` and `"ÉPÉE"` match.
- `label(&self) -> String`: `"<item> x<count>/<max>"`, e.g. `"Apple x3/10"`.

`count ≤ max` is always true for the slots the tests create.
problems.examples_md:
```
Input:  s = Slot { item: "Apple", count: 3, max: 10 }; s.add(5)
Output: 0, and s.count is 8
All 5 fit.

Input:  s = Slot { item: "Apple", count: 8, max: 10 }; s.add(5)
Output: 3, and s.count is 10
Only 2 fit; 3 are left over.

Input:  s = Slot { item: "Arrow", count: 4, max: 20 }; s.take(10)
Output: 4, and s.count is 0
You can't take more than there is.
```

(`"Apple"` stands for `String::from("Apple")`.)

- `0 ≤ count ≤ max ≤ u32::MAX`; `0 ≤ n ≤ u32::MAX`.
- Item names are up to 100 bytes of any Unicode text.
hints: Work out the free space first: `self.max - self.count` can't overflow, but `self.count + n` can.
In `add`, the number that fits is the smaller of `n` and the free space; in `take`, the smaller of `n` and `self.count`.
`let fits = n.min(self.max - self.count); self.count += fits; n - fits`.

- `backspace(&mut self) -> bool`: deletes the character just before the cursor and moves the cursor left by 1. Returns `false` (and changes nothing) when the cursor is at 0.
- `left(&mut self)` and `right(&mut self)`: move the cursor by one character, stopping at the start and the end.
- `home(&mut self)` and `end(&mut self)`: move the cursor to the start (0) or the end (the character count).

Use struct update and explicit cloning to retain independent owned text. retitle consumes its input, changes only the title, and uses struct update without cloning.
problems.constraints_md: All text is valid Unicode, at most 100,000 bytes each; revision accepts all u32 values.
hints: `record` receives owned Strings: put those same-named locals into its fields with shorthand. `revise` receives only a shared borrow, so it cannot move the original body out.
Clone borrowed owned text before struct update; use saturation for the revision.
Override title and revision in revise, then use ..base.clone(); retitle can use ..base without cloning.
problems.solution_approach_md:
Implement record using field init shorthand. revise borrows its input and returns a revision with the supplied title unchanged, the same body, and a saturating increment. Use struct update and explicit cloning to retain independent owned text. retitle consumes its input, changes only the title, and uses struct update without cloning.

Shorthand in record transfers each supplied String without a second allocation. In revise, the shared reference prevents taking the original fields; cloning before update supplies an owned base while the overridden title and revision select the new edition. retitle already owns its input, so update can transfer the untouched body directly. Saturation is necessary because every u32 revision is valid.

problems.title: Reservation ledger
problems.description_md: Create an eight-seat ledger. reserve succeeds only for an in-range vacant seat and stores the id, including id zero. cancel succeeds only for an occupied seat and clears its id. occupied counts used flags. transfer moves an occupied source to a vacant destination; same-seat transfers fail. Every failed operation leaves both arrays unchanged. Use multiple impl blocks, with construction separate from state-changing methods.
problems.constraints_md: Seat indices accept full usize; ids accept full u32. Valid initial state: unused seats have id zero, occupied seats may have any id. Operations preserve this invariant.
hints: The used flag is the source of truth for occupancy. An id of zero may belong to an occupied seat, so counting nonzero ids is incorrect.
Check every failure condition before changing flags or ids.
A successful transfer writes the destination id and flag, then clears the source; occupied scans all eight flags.
problems.solution_approach_md:
Create an eight-seat ledger. reserve succeeds only for an in-range vacant seat and stores the id, including id zero. cancel succeeds only for an occupied seat and clears its id. occupied counts used flags. transfer moves an occupied source to a vacant destination; same-seat transfers fail. A successful transfer copies the id to the destination and then clears the source id and flag. A same-seat destination is occupied, so that operation fails without a special mutation path. Separate impl blocks organize the constructor and operations without creating separate ledgers.

problems.title: Bank account
problems.description_md:
**Part 1 — Construction and inspection:** new trims owner (including Unicode whitespace), permits empty names, starts at zero; summary uses integer money formatting and no final newline.

**Part 2 — Deposit and withdrawal:** zero succeeds; reject insufficient funds or overflow without mutation. All u64 values are supported. Check cents > MAX - balance before addition.

**Part 3 — Transfers:** take exclusive access to two distinct accounts; zero succeeds; reject either source insufficiency or destination overflow before changing either balance. Rust prevents passing one account as both mutable arguments.

**Part 4 — Clone and close:** derived Clone produces independent String ownership and balance values; close consumes self and returns its owner and balance. Moving through returns preserves the owned name. Do not use checked_* APIs requiring Option.
problems.constraints_md: Use the complete numeric ranges above. Text arguments <= 100,000 UTF-8 bytes each; operation fixtures keep account names and book/member text within those bounds. No Unicode normalization or case folding is implied beyond LM4 helpers. Direct public-field values are accepted as described. Runtime tests compare exact text and integer values.
hints: `new` must turn the trimmed owner slice into an owned String. Use `&self` for summary, `&mut self` for balance changes, and owned `self` when returning the name from close.

Before adding cents, compare against `u64::MAX - current_balance`. Before subtracting, compare against available funds. A zero amount satisfies both conditions, including when a balance is already at the maximum.

A transfer needs both checks before either assignment: sufficient source funds and enough destination space. Then subtract and add the same amount. Format money with integer `/ 100`, `% 100`, and a two-digit cent field.
problems.solution_approach_md:
Construct an independent owner String with `owner.trim().to_string()` and set the balance to zero. `deposit` rejects an amount greater than `u64::MAX - self.balance_cents`; otherwise addition is safe. `withdraw` rejects amounts greater than the current balance, then subtracts. Both methods return true for zero without special-case mutation.

`transfer_to` performs both rejection checks before touching either account. Only after they pass does it debit the source and credit the destination, so a failed operation leaves both states unchanged. Ordinary Rust exclusive borrows prevent the same account from being supplied as both receiver and destination.

`summary` borrows the account and uses `format!("{}: ${}.{:02}", self.owner, self.balance_cents / 100, self.balance_cents % 100)`. `close` moves the owner String into its returned tuple; the returned text survives the call. Derived Clone clones each field, producing independent String ownership and an independent copied balance.
problems.idiomatic_md: validate all failure conditions before the first state change. The boolean result communicates acceptance; it must not hide a partially completed transfer.
problems.random_md: Use the problems.md LCG, 300 cases, state reset once at the start. Start two zero-balance accounts. Repeat 40 times: op=pick(3); cents=(next() as u64 << 32) + next(). op 0 deposits into A, 1 withdraws from A, 2 transfers A to B. Model with unbounded mathematical integers, accepting only operations whose resulting balances are in 0..=u64::MAX. Compare each bool and both balances after every operation.

problems.description_md:
**Part 1 — Book:** use the exact supplied derives and fields. new normalizes title via LM4 normalize_title, trims author and retains id/year, accepting every u32/u16. summary is exactly "{title} by {author} ({year})", without newline. Empty strings are permitted.

**Part 2 — Member:** new preserves name exactly and starts borrowed at zero. limit is 3 or 6 for premium. can_borrow means borrowed < limit; record_borrow increments only below limit, otherwise returns false unchanged. record_return decrements a positive count and leaves zero unchanged. All public u8 counts, including 255, are supported.

**Part 3 — Ownership and comparison:** derived Debug, Clone, PartialEq must be present; compare fields, clone both text-bearing types, mutate original and clone independently, and verify non-Copy moves.

**Part 4 — Integration:** start with the LM4 reference baseline below or continue your own Accepted LM4. Preserve all LM4 helpers, LM3 constants/fee functions, and LM2 banner/menu acknowledgements, invalid-input text and EOF-as-Quit. Do not add menu entries, catalogue storage or book status. These APIs are function-tested until later integration.
problems.constraints_md: Use the complete numeric ranges above. Text arguments <= 100,000 UTF-8 bytes each; operation fixtures keep account names and book/member text within those bounds. No Unicode normalization or case folding is implied beyond LM4 helpers. Direct public-field values are accepted as described. Runtime tests compare exact text and integer values.
hints: `Book::new` calls the existing normalize_title helper for its title and trims only the ends of the author. `Member::new` copies the name into owned text exactly as received; it must not share Book's trimming policy.
Implement `limit` as three or six. `can_borrow` compares `borrowed < limit`; `record_borrow` uses that same condition before incrementing, so even a publicly constructed count of 255 cannot overflow.

`record_return` subtracts only when the count is positive. Keep the earlier helpers and menu intact; these types add domain behavior without adding menu commands. Clone fixtures should mutate owned text and counts independently.
problems.solution_approach_md:
`Book::new` builds the exact public fields, normalizing the title through LM4 and trimming the author into an owned String. Its shared `summary` method formats title, author and year with the required separators and no final newline. Public fields remain constructible, so constructor cleanup is not an invariant enforced for every possible Book value.

`Member::new` retains the complete name and begins with zero loans. The shared `limit` and `can_borrow` methods centralize the policy. `record_borrow` returns false immediately when the count is at or above the appropriate limit, otherwise increments and returns true. This ordering handles every u8 count, including 255, without overflow or silently clamping invalid public states. `record_return` decrements a positive count and leaves zero unchanged.

Preserve the exact derives: Debug supplies diagnostic formatting, PartialEq compares fields, and Clone clones Strings independently. Neither type is Copy because it owns String fields. Append the completed types to the supplied LM4 reference starting point and run the inherited helper/menu suites alongside the new member and book tests.
problems.idiomatic_md: use the existing title helper instead of reimplementing a nearly equivalent normalization rule. A small difference in Unicode whitespace behavior would break the continuous project's shared contract.
problems.random_md: Use the problems.md LCG, 300 cases, state reset once at the start. Seed `0x05020000` initializes the common 32-bit LCG once for 300 cases. For each case, draw premium=((next() >> 16) % 2)==1, then borrowed=(next() >> 16) % 256. Construct the initial public Member state with those values, id 7 and name " unchanged ". Repeat exactly 40 operations: draw op=(next() >> 16) % 2; 0 records a borrow and 1 records a return. The upper bits avoid the deterministic alternation of the LCG low bit. Use an unbounded integer model with limit three or six: a borrow succeeds and increments only below the limit, while a return decrements only above zero. Compare each borrow result, can_borrow and the full Member state after every operation. Initial names and ids remain unchanged. Constructor, text and cloning boundaries are covered by the separate exact rows.
